column1: What is the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem requirement, and what artifact results from violating it?
column2: Sampling frequency must exceed twice the highest frequency component in the signal; violating this causes aliasing, where high-frequency components fold down into lower frequency bands, creating spurious artifacts that mimic real physical phenomena.

column1: Why do wheel speed sensors require kilohertz-range sampling rates while coolant temperature sensors can use sampling periods of tens to hundreds of milliseconds?
column2: Wheel speed sensors must capture rapid, transient tire slip events (e.g., lockup during threshold braking), while coolant temperature tracks slow thermal equilibrium over lap-duration timescales, so its signal bandwidth is much lower.

column1: Give a concrete example of aliasing in a racing telemetry context.
column2: An improperly sampled suspension potentiometer during a kerb strike can alias a sharp displacement transient into a false low-frequency oscillation that falsely suggests chassis resonance.

column1: What is the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio for gasoline, and how is it expressed in lambda notation?
column2: 14.7:1 by mass, expressed as λ = 1.0 at stoichiometry.

column1: At what lambda range does an engine produce maximum power, and why?
column2: λ = 0.85 to 0.90 (AFR 12.5:1 to 13.2:1); the excess fuel provides charge cooling that suppresses knock detonation and allows higher ignition advance.

column1: What reluctor wheel pattern is commonly used for crankshaft position sensing, and why is it needed?
column2: A 60-minus-2 reluctor wheel pattern, which provides a missing-tooth reference enabling absolute angular (crank position) determination.

column1: What computational time constraint must an ECU's fuel injection control loop meet at 10,000 RPM in a 4-cylinder engine?
column2: The entire sensing-to-injector-trigger computation chain must complete in under one millisecond to maintain synchronization, since each cylinder fires every 20 milliseconds.

column1: Under what conditions does an ECU operate in open-loop (rather than closed-loop lambda) fueling mode?
column2: During cold starts, wide-open throttle transients, and overrun fuel cut conditions, when oxygen sensor readings are unreliable or transient response is too slow.

column1: What typical thermal efficiency range applies to naturally aspirated vs. turbocharged racing engines?
column2: Naturally aspirated: ~30-40% thermal efficiency; turbocharged: ~35-45% thermal efficiency.

column1: What temperature range do brake rotor surfaces reach during threshold braking from high speed, and what energy transformation causes this?
column2: 600-900°C, caused by the friction brake system converting vehicle kinetic energy into thermal energy at the rotor-pad interface.

column1: What is the 'signal ancestry' invariant in race diagnostics?
column2: Every symptom (wheel lock, overheat, traction loss) has a traceable causal chain from physical root cause through sensors, CAN bus frames, telemetry uplink, to the analysis screen; understanding this chain lets engineers trace symptoms backward to their mechanical origin with precision.

column1: According to the 'gradual before catastrophic' invariant, when does the most valuable diagnostic work occur, and why?
column2: In the 15-20 minutes preceding a catastrophic failure, because degradation curves (e.g., brake pad wear, bearing wear, oil temp rise) are gradual, and this pre-catastrophic window is when low signal-to-noise degradation indicators can still be caught by correctly calibrated thresholds or vigilant engineers.
